sets.title: Know your grid: ERCOT and CAISO side by side
sets.line: Peak demand, generation mix, the battery cycle and carbon intensity, from the latest data.
sets.teacher: About 45 minutes. Prerequisites: MW against MWh, reading a daily and an hourly table. Students should open /grid/ercot, /grid/caiso, /mix, /storage and /emissions, and the tables linked under each question on /data.

questions.q: On the latest day both are held, what was the carbon intensity of generation in ERCOT and in CAISO, and how much higher was ERCOT's?
steps: Read intensity_generation for each grid: the day's CO2 from generation over its net generation.
questions.why: The same kilowatt-hour carries very different emissions depending on where and when it is made.

questions.q: On the latest day both are held, how many MWh did batteries discharge in ERCOT and in CAISO? CAISO's discharge was how many times ERCOT's?
steps: Read mwh_discharged for 2026-11-12 (each grid's local day): ERCOT (eia930:ERCO, EIA-930)
questions.why: Batteries move solar power from midday into the evening peak; how much they discharge shows how far that shift has gone.

day.note: the newest UTC day both eia930_all_demand and eia930_all_generation hold in full (24 hours, both grids)

questions.q: On 2026-11-15 (UTC), the latest day both grids' demand and generation are held in full, what was the highest hour of demand in ERCOT and in CAISO? ERCOT's peak was how many times CAISO's?
steps: Take the 24 hourly demand values of 2026-11-15 (UTC) for each grid (entity eia930:ERCO and eia930:CISO, variable demand_mw).
questions.why: Peak demand, not average demand, sets how much generation and wire a grid has to build.

day.note: the newest UTC day both eia930_all_demand and eia930_all_generation hold in full (24 hours, both grids)

questions.q: On the same day, 2026-11-15 (UTC), what share of each grid's net generation came from natural gas?
steps: Add the 24 hourly values of net_generation_natural_gas_mw and of net_generation_mw for 2026-11-15 (UTC).
questions.why: The fuel that runs most often sets both the price and the emissions of a grid's power.

questions.q: What share of ERCOT's demand on 2026-11-12 (Central time) did its batteries' discharge equal?
steps: Add ERCOT's hourly demand_mw from 2026-11-12T06:00:00Z to 2026-11-13T06:00:00Z (the Central-time day in UTC):
questions.why: Battery output is growing fast, but it is still a small share of all the energy a grid uses.

sets.title: Prices and your bill
sets.line: Load-weighted against simple prices, the shape premium, the wholesale share of two real bills, and the cheapest and dearest hour.
sets.teacher: About 40 minutes. Prerequisites: a weighted average, USD per MWh against cents per kWh (divide by 10). Students should open /cost-of-power, /learn/bill and the method page for the cost of power.

questions.q: For ERCOT's hub average in its latest complete month, what were the load-weighted and the simple average real-time prices, and what is the shape premium?
steps: Load-weighted: each hour's price times ERCOT's demand that hour, over the month's demand:
Simple: the plain mean of the same hours:
questions.why: A grid's load uses power most when it is dear, so its average cost per MWh is above the simple average price.

questions.q: On the default PG&E (California) bill of /learn/bill (600 kWh), how many dollars are wholesale energy, and what share of the bill is that?
questions.why: Most of a home's bill pays for wires, programs and fixed charges, not the power itself; how much differs by state.

questions.q: On the default Oncor (Texas) bill of /learn/bill (600 kWh), how many dollars are wholesale energy, and what share of the bill is that?
questions.why: Most of a home's bill pays for wires, programs and fixed charges, not the power itself; how much differs by state.

questions.q: In the latest complete month of ERCOT's hour-of-day profile, which hour was cheapest and which dearest on average, and how far apart were they?
steps: The latest month every hour of which is held (cost_of_power_monthly: rt_hours equals hours_in_month): 2026-10. Read the 24 values rt_mean_h00 to rt_mean_h23 for that month (Central time).
questions.why: The daily price swing is what a battery, or a flexible load, earns by moving use.

questions.q: The table's public rows hold 6 hubs: CAISO NP15, CAISO SP15, ERCOT hub average, ercot:LZ_HOUSTON, ercot:LZ_NORTH, SPP North hub. In the latest month all 6 hold at least 95 percent of their hours, which had the largest shape premium, and which the smallest?
steps: Find the latest month in which every hub's rt_hours is at least 95 percent of its hours_in_month: 2026-09.
Read rt_shape_premium of each hub for that month:
questions.why: Where the premium is large, shifting use out of peak hours saves the most.

sets.title: When the grid broke: four events
sets.line: Winter Storm Uri, CAISO's August 2020 heat, Winter Storm Elliott and ERCOT's 2023 heat, one question each and one comparing two.
sets.teacher: About 50 minutes. Prerequisites: percent change, a baseline (the same weekdays of earlier years). Students should open /events and the four event pages, and read each page's note on what contradicted the headline story.

questions.q: Winter Storm Elliott (December 2022): what was PJM's highest hour of demand served in the window, on which day, and how far above the same weekdays of 2021 and 2020 was that day's peak?
steps: Read demand_max_mw (event elliott_2022, eia930:PJM) from 2022-12-19 on and find the highest:
questions.why: Winter peaks can rival summer ones when a cold snap meets electric heating and failing plants.

questions.q: CAISO, August 2020: on which day was the peak hour furthest above the same weekdays of earlier years, and by how many percentage points did it exceed 2020-08-14, the first day of rotating outages?
steps: Read demand_max_pct_vs_baseline (event caiso_heat_2020) for each day and find the highest:
questions.why: The outages came before demand peaked: supply fell short, not demand alone.

questions.q: ERCOT, summer 2023: on which day was the highest 15-minute real-time price, and on which day the highest hour of demand? Were they the same day?
steps: Read rt_max (event ercot_heat_2023) and find the highest:
Read demand_max_mw and find the highest:
questions.why: Prices spike when supply is short, which is not always when demand is highest: wind and the solar ramp at sunset matter too.

questions.q: Winter Storm Uri (ERCOT, February 2021): the highest 15-minute real-time price during the storm window was how many times the highest on the same days of 2019 and 2020?
steps: Read rt_max (event uri_2021, ercot:HB_HUBAVG) for every day; the highest in 2021 is
The highest on the 2019 and 2020 days is
questions.why: Scarcity pricing lets the price rise to the cap when supply fails, which is the market's signal and the customer's risk.

questions.q: Compare two ERCOT events: Winter Storm Uri's highest 15-minute real-time price was how many times the summer 2023 heat's?
questions.why: Both hit the price cap's neighborhood, but Uri held prices there for days and cut power to millions.

sets.title: Storage and taxes
sets.line: How much energy ERCOT's batteries give back, when they charge and discharge, what one home battery cycle earns, and the oil and gas production taxes of three states.
sets.teacher: About 45 minutes. Prerequisites: MWh against kWh, a percent of value, a round trip efficiency. Students should open /storage, /play/battery, /cost-of-power and /severance, and read the cited rule behind each tax.

questions.q: On 2026-11-12, at which hour (Central time) did ERCOT's batteries charge hardest, at which did they discharge hardest, and how many hours apart were they?
steps: Read peak_charge_hour and peak_discharge_hour for that day (the hour starting, 0 to 23, local time).
questions.why: Batteries fill when solar floods the grid at midday and empty into the evening peak, when the sun has set and demand is still high.

questions.q: Over the seven latest days held (2026-11-06 to 2026-11-12), how much energy did ERCOT's batteries discharge and charge, and what share of the energy in came back out? How does that compare with the game's battery?
steps: Add ERCOT's (eia930:ERCO) daily mwh_discharged and mwh_charged over 2026-11-06 to 2026-11-12 (local days).
The game's battery is an assumption:
questions.why: Every battery loses some energy in the round trip; a single day's ratio can even pass 100 percent when a charge and its discharge fall on different days, so a week is fairer.

questions.q: A well produces 1,000 barrels of oil in 2026-10, valued at that month's WTI Cushing mean. What state production tax does it owe in Texas, in Louisiana (a well completed before July 2025, no transport deducted) and in New Mexico (no royalty, trucking or district ad valorem)?
steps: The mean of 2026-10's daily WTI Cushing spot prices:
Texas: 4.6 percent of value, or 4.6 cents a barrel if more:

New Mexico: severance 3.75, emergency school 3.15, conservation 0.24 percent of value, the rates the rules file states for 2026-04-01 to 2026-08-31 (TRD table) (the newest it holds; 2026-10 is later):
questions.why: The same barrel pays very different taxes across a state line. Each rate cites its statute or agency page on /severance.

questions.q: The home battery game's battery charges once from empty at ERCOT's cheapest average hour of 2026-10 (the latest complete month) and empties at its dearest. What does that one cycle earn, and what would the game's fictional fleet of homes earn?
steps: The cheapest hour of the month's profile is 11:00,
To store 13.5 kWh at 90 percent round trip (the square root of 0.9 each way) it buys
questions.why: The price spread between hours is a battery's whole business, and a home battery's share of it is small: what matters is scale.

questions.q: A Texas gas well produced 2,400 Mcf in 2026-08 (77.4 Mcf a day over its 31 days), valued at that month's Henry Hub mean. What is its tax, and what does it owe with the low-producing well credit?
steps: The mean of 2026-08's daily Henry Hub spot prices, applied per Mcf:
The well averages 90 Mcf a day or less, so it may claim the credit, set by the Comptroller's certified price for the month in 2005 dollars:
questions.why: Low-producing wells get tax relief when prices are low, so they are not plugged for good; the test uses a certified price, not the well's own.

sets.title: Networks and money
sets.line: ERCOT's ties and the biggest exporter in the network's newest hour, a solar plant's capture rate, a battery's debt cover, and what a plant earned in Winter Storm Uri.
sets.teacher: About 45 minutes. Prerequisites: MW against MWh, a weighted price, a ratio. Students should open /network (pick ERCOT, slide to the last hour), /cost-of-power/seller (solar, then battery, at ERCOT) and the Uri event page. The network's hour moves as the hourly refresh runs; the money questions move when the seller's snapshot is rebuilt.

questions.q: A merchant solar plant at ERCOT's hub average (HB_HUBAVG) sells every MWh it makes at the real-time price. In 2026-09, the latest complete month held, what price did its output capture, and what is that as a share of the month's flat (time-average) price?
steps: Capture price: the month's revenue from its sales over the MWh it made (the Texas solar fleet's hourly shape, per MW of nameplate):
Flat price: the mean of every hour's real-time price in the month:
questions.why: Solar makes its power when every other solar plant does, so midday prices sag and a solar MWh is worth less than the average MWh. The capture rate measures that discount.

questions.q: In the newest hour of the network snapshot, 2026-11-18 04:00 UTC (Nov 17, 23:00 Eastern), with how many neighboring balancing authorities did ERCOT exchange power, and what was the largest flow?
line: count of ERCOT's ties with a flow =
steps: On /network, pick ERCOT and set the slider to the last hour; or read the snapshot's links that have ERCO at either end, in that hour.
Count the neighbors with a reported flow:
Southwest Power Pool (SWPP), Centro Nacional de Control de Energia (CEN)
The largest in size, whichever way it runs:

questions.why: ERCOT is almost an island: its grid is an interconnection of its own, joined to its neighbors only through a few direct-current ties (each neighbor here may be several of them), so it cannot lean on them much in an emergency.

questions.q: In the same hour, which balancing authority exported the most power, net, to its neighbors?
answer: Salt River Project Agricultural Improvement and Power District (SRP), a net export of
line: the largest, over every balancing authority, of the sum of its tie flows =
steps: For each balancing authority, add the flows on all its ties in that hour, exports positive and imports negative.
Salt River Project Agricultural Improvement and Power District (SRP),

The sum covers the ties between balancing authorities in the snapshot; EIA's regions and its country totals are left out, since they repeat the same flows.
questions.why: A net exporter has more generation than load in that hour, often cheap hydro, wind or solar, and its ties carry the surplus to where it is worth more.

questions.q: A default merchant battery at ERCOT's hub average, 100 MW / 400 MWh, financed with 60 percent debt at 8 percent over its 20-year life at Lazard's midpoint cost, owes 6,783,357 USD of debt service a year. In how many of the months held, 2018-07 to 2026-09, could its cash flow at best cover that month's share?
answer: even with perfect foresight. A real battery, which cannot see the day's prices in advance, earns less and covers fewer.
steps: Each month: the battery's arbitrage revenue (one cycle a day with perfect foresight, an upper bound) less fixed O&M, over one twelfth of the annual debt service: the debt service coverage ratio.
At best, because the revenue is an upper bound, as the seller's tab notes: the battery knows each day's prices in advance; a real one captures a fraction of this.
questions.why: A lender looks at the bad months, not the average: a battery's revenue comes in bursts, a few price spikes a year, and the months between them must still pay the debt.

questions.q: During Winter Storm Uri, February 2021 (the 18 days from 2021-02-07 to 2021-02-24), what did the same 100 MW merchant solar plant at ERCOT's hub average earn, against as many normal days before the storm?
steps: Each day's revenue: the plant's hourly output (the fleet's shape that day) times the hour's real-time price, added up.
A normal day: the mean of the baseline days of the same event (the same dates of earlier years):
. A normal week is seven of them,
As many normal days as the storm lasted:
questions.why: Scarcity pays whoever can deliver in it. Uri's prices sat at the cap for days, so even a plant whose output fell with the snow and the short days could earn more in the storm than on as many normal days.

sets.title: Who trades with whom: power between regions

sets.title: What is under the ground and in the wind
sets.line: The resource map's layers read in their own units: the wind and the sun, a modelled wind farm's capacity factor, geothermal sites, power that dams without turbines could make, and biomass counted in tonnes.
sets.teacher: About 40 minutes. Prerequisites: a unit and what it measures (m/s, kWh per square metre per day, MW, MWh, tonnes), a ratio, a share. Students should open the resources tab of /map, switch each layer on and read its legend, and open the Method note at the foot for each layer's unit, vintage and grain. Some figures (a layer's totals) are in the list of layers itself, site/data/resources/manifest.json.

questions.q: Two solar layers share a unit (kWh/m2/day): "Global Horizontal Irradiance" and "Direct Normal Irradiance". What is the highest value of each legend, and the second's is how many times the first's?
steps: Switch on each layer in turn and read the legend's top, or the layers solar_ghi and solar_dni, legend, max:
questions.why: Global horizontal irradiance is the sunlight on a flat surface; direct normal irradiance is the beam on a surface turned to face the sun. In a clear desert the direct beam is the larger, which is why plants that track the sun or concentrate it are built there.

questions.q: The layer "Wind speed at 100 m": what is the highest value of its legend, what is the highest value in the source's own cells (the list's source_stats, max), and how far apart are they? Why is the map's lower?
answer: , because each map cell is the mean of the source's cells inside it.
steps: Switch on Wind speed at 100 m and read the legend's top; or the layer wind_speed_100m, legend, max:
The source's own grain is 2 km ("2km x 2km"); the list's source_stats, max, is the highest of its cells:
. The Method note says a coarser cell is the mean of the source's cells inside it, and a mean is never above the highest of what it averages.
questions.why: A map has to average a fine source into larger cells, which lowers the peaks: the windiest spot is windier than any cell of the map shows.

questions.q: The layer "Wind capacity factor (supply curve sites)" (Mean capacity factor across 11.5km grid-cell (the source's capacity_factor_ac)) is a ratio. What are the mean and the highest values the list gives for it, and the highest is how many times the mean?
answer: Even there a wind farm makes less in a year than it would at full power every hour.
steps: In site/data/resources/manifest.json, the layer wind_capacity_factor, stats: mean
. The legend on the map runs to the same top.
A capacity factor is the energy a plant makes over the energy it would make at full power every hour: a ratio, so multiply by 100 for a percent.
questions.why: Nameplate megawatts are not energy: a wind farm's output follows the wind, so the energy it makes in a year is its capacity times the hours times its capacity factor.

questions.q: The layer "Solid biomass resources by county" is counted in dry metric tons/year. What is its national total, how much of it is crop residue (the part CropRes), and what share is that?
answer: . A tonne is a mass, not energy: the map does not say how much power it would make.
steps: In site/data/resources/manifest.json, the layer biomass: national_total
questions.why: To turn tonnes into energy needs the heat in each kind of biomass and the efficiency of the plant that burns it, which the layer does not give; a figure in the wrong unit cannot be compared with a power plant.

questions.q: The layer "Identified hydrothermal systems": how many sites does it hold, what is the sum of their estimated output (Mean Megawatts electric (MWe), the source's MWe_Mean), the largest site's, and what share of the sum is the largest?
steps: In site/data/resources/manifest.json, the layer geothermal_hydrothermal_sites: stats, n,
questions.why: MWe is megawatts of electricity a resource is estimated to support (U.S. Geological Survey (USGS)), not a plant that exists: a resource estimate says what could be built, and much of it may never be.

questions.q: The layer "Hydropower potential at non-powered dams" holds dams that make no power today. What capacity and what yearly energy does it estimate for them in all, and how many hours of full output a year is that energy?
steps: In site/data/resources/manifest.json, the layer hydropower_npd: total_cap_mw
MWh divided by MW is hours:
, the hours the dams would need at full power to make a year's energy.
questions.why: Hours of full output set against all the hours of a year are a capacity factor in another form: an estimate of energy, from a capacity that is not built.

questions.why: Electricity loses energy on its way from the power plant: the sector's total counts its share of those losses, and its end use counts only what reached it.

questions.q: How much energy did the industrial sector consume in July 2026 and in July 2025, a year before, and the first is how many times the second?
steps: monthly, by_source, total at positions 642 (2026-07) and 630 (2025-07).
questions.why: A month is set against the same month of the year before, so the season is the same on both sides and only the year differs.

questions.q: The industries ranked by fuel consumption in 2022: which two used the most, how much did each use, and the first's is how many times the second's?
steps: industries, ranked_3_digit, lists the industries from the largest: 325 (Chemicals) and 324 (Petroleum and Coal Products) first.
questions.why: A few industries that turn raw materials into chemicals, fuels, paper and metals use most of manufacturing's energy; most others use far less.

questions.q: Chemicals in 2022: how much fuel did its plants in the South census region consume, of how much in the United States, and what share is that?
questions.why: An industry settles where its raw materials, its fuel and its customers are, so one census region can hold most of an industry's energy use.

questions.q: Petroleum and Coal Products in 2022: how much of its fuel does the survey count as "other", of how much in all, and what share is that?
questions.why: The survey names a column for each common fuel; "other" holds what has no column of its own, which for a refinery includes fuels it makes from its own crude oil, so a large "other" is not an unknown.

questions.why: A state's industrial energy follows its refineries and chemical plants more than its population, so a smaller state can use a large share.

questions.q: Chemicals in 2022: how much electricity did its plants generate on site, what was its net demand for electricity, and what share of the net demand is the on-site generation?
questions.why: Many large plants burn fuel to make both steam and electricity (cogeneration), so part of their electricity never passes through the grid and is not in the utilities' sales.

sets.title: Your own balancing authority: what it owns, what is coming, how clean it is, whom it leans on
sets.line: The Tennessee Valley Authority's power plants and its largest, what it plans to build and retire, what its nuclear and gas plants generated against what they could, the neighbour it imports from, two grids' carbon side by side, and how fast its demand grew.
sets.teacher: About 45 minutes. Prerequisites: MW against MWh, a share, a ratio, a difference in percentage points. Students open the Grid tool's map (/grid, the network view, Map), click the Tennessee Valley Authority and read the block Its own facts; then repeat any question for the authority they live in, from its own file under site/data/regions/authority/. The worked answers read site/data/regions/authority/tva.json, erco.json and ciso.json.

questions.q: Which is the Tennessee Valley Authority's largest power plant, how much capacity does it have, and what share of the authority's capacity is that?
steps: owns, largest_plants lists the ten largest plants from the largest: the first is
questions.why: A few large plants hold much of an authority's capacity, so the loss of one of them on a cold morning is felt across the whole authority.

questions.q: For the Tennessee Valley Authority, what share of its capacity is nuclear and what share is natural gas, and what share of its generation from November 2025 to October 2026 did each make? Which fleet runs harder?
answer: Nuclear makes the larger share of generation for its share of capacity: it runs nearly every hour, gas plants run when they are needed.
steps: Generation shares from burns, share_pct, over November 2025 to October 2026: nuclear
Compare each fleet's share of generation with its share of capacity.
questions.why: Capacity says what a fleet could make in an hour; generation says what it made. A fleet whose share of generation is above its share of capacity runs more of the year than the others.

questions.q: Over November 2025 to October 2026, how much CO2 did each MWh generated in ERCOT and in CAISO carry, by EIA's estimates, and ERCOT's is how many times CAISO's? Why does the Tennessee Valley Authority's file give no figure?
answer: The Tennessee Valley Authority's file says why it has none: EIA's hourly CO2 estimates held by the ERW (eia930_all_emissions, from EIA's Grid Monitor workbooks) cover the seven ISOs and the Lower 48 only.
steps: In site/data/regions/authority/erco.json and ciso.json: burns, co2, intensity_kg_per_mwh:
In tva.json, burns, co2, intensity_kg_per_mwh is empty and burns, co2, why gives the reason.
questions.why: The carbon a MWh carries follows the mix: more coal and gas, more CO2. A blank with its reason is a fact too: the estimate is not held for that authority, which is not the same as zero.
